---
title: "Mathematics for Machine Learning: Introduction"
description: "Why vectors, models, and parameter learning belong in one conceptual framework."
---

## The question

A prediction system for an online shop has recorded six orders. For each one, we know the **delivery distance** $d$, **item count** $n$ and **fulfilment time** $t$. Our goal is to make predictions for orders not yet observed.

We need three distinct ideas:

1. **Data:** observations $\mathcal D=\{(\boldsymbol x_i,t_i)\}$, where $\boldsymbol x_i=(d_i,n_i)^\top$.
2. **Model:** a family of functions $f_{\theta}(\boldsymbol x)$ that produces a predicted time.
3. **Learning:** an algorithm that selects parameters $\theta$ by assessing observations against a defined objective.

The separation matters because even a perfectly implemented optimisation algorithm cannot repair a misleading dataset or an unsuitable model family.

## One small equation linking the ideas

$$
\hat\theta=\arg\min_{\theta}\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N
\bigl(f_{\theta}(\boldsymbol x_i)-t_i\bigr)^2.
$$

The sum uses **training data** to select parameters. We still need a validation/test design to check whether the model predicts future orders reliably. The formula is an example of empirical risk minimisation, not a claim that all machine learning is squared-error regression.

## Two complementary learning routes

**Bottom-up:** study linear algebra and geometry, then calculus, probability and optimisation, before studying regression, PCA, mixtures and classification. This route is useful when unfamiliar symbols are the main obstacle.

**Top-down:** start with a real prediction problem, ask why a particular algorithm needs an eigenvector or a gradient, then follow the links back to the mathematical prerequisites. This route provides immediate motivation.

The book *Mathematics for Machine Learning* describes both reading styles and divides its material into **Mathematical Foundations** and **Central Machine Learning Problems**. Our knowledge library keeps that relationship but uses an independent running example and original content.

## Symbol conventions

| Notation | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $a, b, t$ | Scalars |
| $\boldsymbol x\in\mathbb R^D$ | A feature vector with $D$ coordinates |
| $X\in\mathbb R^{N\times D}$ | $N$ observations with $D$ features |
| $\theta$ | Model parameters |
| $\nabla f$ | Gradient |
| $\mathbb E[X]$ | Expected value of a random variable |
| $\arg\min f$ | Inputs that minimise $f$ |

Use the [Python lab](../../examples/README.md) with all its modes to observe how a single dataset connects these concepts. (The first command below is run from repository root.)

~~~bash
python3 ai-mathematics/examples/delivery_ml_lab.py all
~~~
